To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a new operational mean-sea-level pressure versus maximum near-surface wind formula has been developed that incorporates latitude, size and storm motion and is based on a modified approach recently developed by Dr Knaff and Dr Zehr; 2) a weakness of the original Knaff-Zehr formulation for storms at low latitude has been identified and rectified in our derivation; and 3) the new approach has potential to be used to reanalyse historical events.

a wind-pressure relationship based on Knaff and Zher’s approach, but incorporating a latitude correction and a radius of gales correction, provides a good approximation to the central pressure for tropical cyclones, and can be readily integrated into an operational environment.
the Knaff andZehr relationship for the wind-pressure relationship is modified to incorporate storm size and storm motion and is suitable for implementation in an operational environment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new wind-pressure relationship for the operational determination of tropical cyclone central pressure.
the derivation of a mean sea-level pressure for a tropical cyclone from the maximum near-surface wind speed.

improving the accuracy and efficiency of the calculation of the mean sea-level pressure in tropical cyclone warning centres, and the potential to reanalyze past events in the context of a new wind-pressure relationship.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a need for caution in the use of wind-pressure relationships to estimate central pressures in the Australian region, particularly at weaker intensities.
, while the wind-pressure relationship has some value, it is not the best way to derive a central pressure.
the Dvorak CI numbers for tropical cyclones in the Atlantic basin are more accurate for stronger storms, but are less accurate at weaker intensities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the new algorithm should result in a more accurate determination of central pressure and hence intensity, and should result in more consistent intensity estimates for the Australian region.

the new wind-pressure relationship is more robust, particularly for low-latitude storms, and the new methodology provides a more consistent approach to determining the central pressure for tropical cyclone basing on the available information.
the new wind-pressure relationship is a significant improvement over the existing Australian operational method.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the wind pressure relationship developed by Knaff (2007), and modified in this study, can be used operationally to derive the central pressure of a tropical cyclone.
a new operational wind-pressure relationship is now available for use in Tropical Cyclones Warning Centres and the potential to re-analyse past events is now available.
